lead: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction that turns injected electrons into spontaneous photons. Its chip structure decides how many photons escape, and its efficiency decides how much optical power reaches a fiber. LEDs are used in short-distance links, local area networks, sensors and displays because they are cheap, reliable and need simple drive circuits. This chapter covers planar, dome, surface-emitter and edge-emitter LEDs, then the efficiencies, I-P curve, spectrum, modulation bandwidth and temperature behaviour that set their use.
prereq: You need spontaneous emission and direct-bandgap recombination from 3.1; numerical aperture from Unit 1 is used later in 3.6.

blocks.text: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction. In a direct-bandgap semiconductor such as GaAs, electrons and holes recombine spontaneously and release photons. A double heterostructure places a thin active layer between wider-bandgap p and n confining layers. This traps carriers in the active layer and improves injection. The chip shape then decides how light leaves.

A planar LED is the simplest surface emitter. The active layer sits near the top surface and light exits through that surface. Total internal reflection traps much of the light because the semiconductor has a high refractive index. A dome LED shapes the chip into a hemisphere or adds a dome lens. Rays meet the surface more nearly at right angles, so more light escapes.

A higher-radiance surface emitter, called a Burrus LED in some syllabi, uses a small active area and a substrate window or well so light leaves from one face. It gives a small, bright emitting spot and couples well to a fiber. An edge emitter LED guides light along a stripe to a cleaved edge. Its emitting area is narrow and directional, so coupling is better than a simple planar LED. It still emits spontaneous light, not laser light.

Three efficiencies are easy to mix. Internal quantum efficiency η_int is the number of photons generated in the active region per electron injected. Extraction efficiency η_extraction is the number of photons escaping the chip per photon generated inside. External quantum efficiency η_ext is the number of photons escaping per electron injected:
η_int = N_ph(int)/N_e,   η_ext = η_int × η_extraction,   η_power = P_out/(I V)
blocks.where: N_ph(int) is photons generated per second; N_e is electrons injected per second; P_out is escaping optical power in W; I is forward current in A; V is forward voltage in V. η_power is wall-plug power efficiency.

blocks.text: Power efficiency includes electrical losses, so it is lower than η_ext. The I-P curve plots P_out against I. Above turn-on it is almost linear. The slope is:
P_out = η_ext (I/e) E,   dP_out/dI = η_ext E/e
blocks.where: E is photon energy in J; e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge.

blocks.text: Linear power against current lets you modulate an LED by changing its drive current. A planar LED with η_int = 0.70 and η_extraction = 0.20 has η_ext = 0.14; 14% of injected electrons give escaping photons. The rest become heat or trapped light.

An LED emits over a band of wavelengths, not one line. Recombination involves a spread of carrier energies and a thermal distribution, so the spectrum has a full width at half maximum of tens of nanometres. This width causes chromatic dispersion in a fiber, so LEDs suit short links. See Unit 2 for dispersion.

Speed is limited by the carrier lifetime τ. A rough modulation bandwidth is f₃dB ≈ 1/(2πτ), where τ is in seconds and f₃dB is in hertz. A shorter lifetime means faster modulation. LEDs reach tens to a few hundred MHz, well below a laser diode.

Temperature changes both power and wavelength. As temperature rises, non-radiative recombination increases, so output power falls. The bandgap shrinks, so the peak wavelength shifts to longer wavelengths. Drive circuits use temperature compensation or a monitor photodiode when output must stay steady.

examples.question: A planar LED has internal quantum efficiency 0.70 and extraction efficiency 0.20. It is driven by a forward current of 50 mA. Each emitted photon has energy 1.4 eV. Take e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J. Find (a) the number of photons generated per second inside the chip, (b) the number leaving the chip per second, and (c) the external optical power in mW.
steps: Convert current: I = 50 mA = 50×10⁻³ A = 0.050 A.
Electrons injected per second = I/e = 0.050/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 3.125×10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Photons generated inside = η_int × electrons/s = 0.70 × 3.125×10¹⁷ = 2.1875×10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Photons escaping = η_extraction × photons inside = 0.20 × 2.1875×10¹⁷ = 4.375×10¹⁶ s⁻¹. External quantum efficiency = 0.70 × 0.20 = 0.14.
P_out = escaping photons/s × photon energy = 4.375×10¹⁶ × 2.24×10⁻¹⁹ = 9.80×10⁻³ W = 9.80 mW.
examples.answer: The external optical power is about 9.8 mW.

traps: Do not multiply by extraction efficiency twice. External efficiency already contains η_int and η_extraction; use P_out = η_ext (I/e) E once.
Keep current in amperes when using e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C. 50 mA is 0.050 A, not 50.
Convert photon energy from eV to joules before calculating watts: 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
External quantum efficiency and power efficiency are different. η_ext counts photons per electron; η_power divides optical watts by electrical watts.
An edge emitter LED is not a laser. It is still spontaneous emission; laser action needs feedback and threshold, covered in 3.3–3.4.

quiz.q: Define internal quantum efficiency of an LED.
quiz.a: It is the number of photons generated in the active region per electron injected into the diode.

quiz.q: Why does a planar LED have lower extraction efficiency than a dome LED?
quiz.a: In a planar LED many rays hit the top surface beyond the critical angle and suffer total internal reflection. The dome shape makes rays meet the surface more nearly normally, so fewer are trapped.

quiz.q: An LED has η_int = 0.80, η_extraction = 0.25, forward current 40 mA and photon energy 2.0 eV. Find the external optical power in mW. Take e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Give two reasons why an LED's output power falls as temperature rises.
quiz.a: Non-radiative recombination and carrier leakage increase with temperature, reducing internal quantum efficiency. The bandgap also shrinks, which shifts the emission to longer wavelength and can reduce emission at the design wavelength.

quiz.q: State the difference between external quantum efficiency and power efficiency.
quiz.a: External quantum efficiency is escaping photons per injected electron. Power efficiency is emitted optical power divided by electrical input power (I V).

quiz.q: An LED has a linear I-P slope of 0.20 W/A. Find the optical power for a current of 30 mA above turn-on.
Why does an edge emitter LED couple better to a fiber than a planar LED?
quiz.a: Its emitting area is narrow and its light is guided along a stripe, so the output has a smaller area and a narrower angular spread. This raises radiance and matches the fiber core and numerical aperture better.

beyond: Not for the exam. LEDs now appear in visible-light communication, where room lights carry data, and in plastic-optical-fiber links inside cars and homes. Blue and white GaN LEDs changed lighting, and micro-LEDs are being developed for displays. Researchers work on improving extraction with photonic crystals and surface textures, and on faster LEDs by shortening carrier lifetime. Search terms: Burrus LED, resonant-cavity LED, micro-LED, visible light communication.
